common_name: Shooting Star Gardenia (Cold-Hardy Large Single-Flowered Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil sited out of harsh winter wind; Shooting Star traces to seed collected at the Beijing Botanical Garden and carries some of the best cold tolerance of any common gardenia cultivar.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, sheltered from drying winter winds that can scorch the dark, glossy foliage. Shooting Star produces large, single, star-shaped white flowers up to three inches across with a strong classic gardenia fragrance, and its compact, rounded habit stays tidier than many older double-flowered selections. Its standout trait is winter hardiness at the cold edge of the gardenia range, making it a good candidate for gardens where other cultivars struggle to overwinter. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer during the growing season and keep soil evenly moist to prevent bud drop and chlorosis.

common_name: Scentsation Gardenia (Southern Living Extended-Bloom Fragrant Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil sited away from competitive tree roots and near a walkway, window, or patio where the heavy fragrance can be enjoyed.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to moderate shade, working in compost or an acid-forming fertilizer at planting. Scentsation is part of the Southern Living Plant Collection and is prized for exceptionally heavy fragrance carried by glossy dark-green foliage, with blooms beginning in late spring and continuing intermittently into fall. Avoid fertilizing after late summer, since the resulting flush of tender new growth is prone to winter dieback, and prune only after flowering to preserve next season's buds. Consistent moisture and acidic soil prevent the interveinal yellowing gardenias show when grown in alkaline conditions.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Radicans Variegata Gardenia (Variegated Dwarf Creeping Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in light to moderate shade; the low, spreading, horizontally branching habit makes it a natural low border or container edger rather than an upright hedge plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in light to moderate shade, protected from competing tree roots. Radicans Variegata is a sport of the dwarf creeping Radicans gardenia, distinguished by glossy dark-green leaves edged in creamy white that provide year-round interest even between bloom cycles. Small, intensely fragrant white flowers appear in spring and summer against the variegated foliage, and the low, wide-spreading habit suits container plantings, small-space groundcover, and edging along shaded paths. Keep soil consistently moist and feed with an acid-forming fertilizer during the growing season to prevent chlorosis and support reliable flowering.

common_name: Grif's Select Gardenia (Compact Small-Leaved Cold-Hardy Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; traces to seed the late Michael Dirr collected at the Beijing Botanic Garden and was introduced through the J.C. Raulston Arboretum at NC State University.

directions: Grif's Select produces single, daisy-like fragrant white flowers up to 3 inches across in summer, opening on a compact, small-leaved plant only 3 to 4 feet tall and wide. Showy red-orange seed capsules follow the flowers and persist into winter, adding color after bloom. It traces to seed the late plantsman Michael Dirr collected at the Beijing Botanic Garden and was introduced through the J.C. Raulston Arboretum at NC State University. Among the most cold-hardy gardenias available, it is reliably grown in zone 7 and has been reported by growers to survive zone 6 winters with some protection.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service
J.C. Raulston Arboretum, NC State University

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; this cultivar is named for the influential Texas and Gulf South plantsman Lynn Lowrey.

directions: Lynn Lowrey bears fragrant white flowers accented with a buttery-yellow eye at the center, a distinctive look among gardenia cultivars. It flowers from early to midsummer on a dense, upright, multi-stemmed evergreen shrub with glossy dark green foliage. The cultivar honors Lynn Lowrey, the influential Texas and Gulf South plantsman and nurseryman known for championing tough native and adapted plants in Southern gardens. Give it the same acidic, moisture-retentive soil and partial shade other gardenias need for the best flowering.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
J.C. Raulston Arboretum, NC State University

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade with consistent moisture; selected by Joseph and Debbie Powell of Columbus, Georgia, and named for their son.

directions: Michael produces enormous fragrant white flowers at least 5 inches across from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, moderately fast-growing shrub that can reach 6 feet tall and wide. Its glossy forest-green leaves are unusually large, in keeping with the oversized flowers. The cultivar was selected by Joseph and Debbie Powell of Columbus, Georgia, and named for their son. It is regarded as one of the most cold-hardy gardenias, commonly recommended for USDA zone 6 in a sheltered site with consistent watering.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service
J.C. Raulston Arboretum, NC State University

common_name: Double Mint Gardenia (Compact Reblooming Double-Flowered Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; a patented First Editions introduction bred for a compact, cold-resistant habit.

directions: Double Mint bears large, double, intensely fragrant white flowers about 2 inches across in a heavy spring flush with a repeat bloom in fall. It forms a compact, rounded evergreen shrub only about 3 feet tall and wide, with glossy dark-green foliage that holds its color through winter. Marketed as a patented First Editions plant introduction, it is described as fully cold-resistant in zone 7. Grow it in morning sun with afternoon shade for the best flowering and foliage color.

common_name: Fragrant Pathways Gardenia (Low Spreading Groundcover Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in mostly sun to dappled shade; an especially cold-hardy, low-spreading sport of Gardenia jasminoides var. radicans.

directions: Fragrant Pathways is an exceptionally low, spreading form of dwarf gardenia, growing only about 8 to 24 inches tall while spreading 3 to 4 feet as a groundcover. It produces fragrant, double white flowers in late spring and early summer above narrow, fine-textured dark green foliage. Selected as an especially cold-hardy sport of Gardenia jasminoides var. radicans, it works well along walkways, between stepping stones, or massed as a fragrant low edging. It is heat- and humidity-tolerant and hardy across USDA zones 7 to 10.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home and Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; one of the few Japanese-named variegated gardenia selections, with fukurin referring to its marginal leaf variegation.

directions: Fukurinkoba is a Japanese cultivar selected for its variegated foliage, with leaves sized like Mystery but colored pewter-green and edged in creamy white margins. Its single, fragrant white flowers open in the typical late-spring-to-summer gardenia season on a rounded 3- to 4-foot shrub. Among variegated gardenias it is noted for standing out in winter hardiness, tolerating full winter sun exposure with little foliage damage where other variegated forms struggle. The bold leaf variegation makes it a foliage-first choice as much as a flowering one.

common_name: Fool Proof Gardenia (Disease-Resistant Compact Double-Flowered Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; a patented Southern Living Plant Collection hybrid gardenia bred for reliable performance.

directions: Fool Proof produces fragrant, fully double white flowers from late spring through fall on a compact plant bred for reliable, disease-resistant garden performance. Mature plants form a dense, rounded shrub only about 3 to 4 feet tall and wide with glossy deep-green evergreen foliage. Part of the Southern Living Plant Collection and patented as Gardenia hybrid Leesix, it is rated hardy to USDA zone 7, with growers in colder zones advised to keep it in containers that can be moved indoors for winter. It tolerates full sun to partial shade and shows good drought tolerance once established.

common_name: Pillow Talk Gardenia (Spreading Mounded Double-Flowered Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; marketed by Proven Winners under the cultivar code SMNGDUO and has an unusually wide, spreading habit.

directions: Pillow Talk carries large, fully double, pure white flowers with classic heavy gardenia fragrance, smothering the plant during a heavy spring-to-early-summer bloom. It has an unusual spreading, mounding habit that grows wider than tall, reaching only about 2.5 to 3.5 feet high but 3 to 4 feet wide. Marketed by Proven Winners under the cultivar code SMNGDUO, it is hardy from USDA zone 7 to 9, with overwintering flower buds reported to survive into zone 6b on a site sheltered from winter wind. Plant it in partial shade with consistently moist, acidic soil for the heaviest bloom.
